name: Patrick Collison
notice: Simulation based on public material; not the person's own words.

D01.one_line: The door to frontier pre-training is left basically only to big companies; what academia can do is the narrow-domain, open-weights, evaluated kind
D01.late_modes: Simply reproducing or catching up with frontier pre-training: the resource threshold is locked up by big companies, and academia cannot catch up
D01.conflict: Meta board member; Meta runs its own large-scale pre-training (Llama)

D02.one_line: AI can probably run existing post-training pipelines more skillfully, but this looks more like execution getting cheaper than a new paradigm

D03.one_line: Long-horizon credit assignment and continual learning are unsolved and a more lasting bottleneck than post-training, but my evidence is thin

D04.one_line: My own company's data (more than 600 AI-written PRs, only 1 rolled back) shows that the execution side is being absorbed quickly and the window is closing fast
D04.late_modes: General agent scaffolding and harnesses: absorbed by frontier models themselves, and Stripe's own experience is the evidence
D04.conflict: Stripe uses AI heavily to write code; invested in Cursor's parent company via a16z

D05.one_line: Verification is the bottleneck I keep talking about; LMArena going from a Berkeley project to a company shows that academia can build things that really get adopted

D06.one_line: One of the directions with the thinnest material; real-robot data and hardware look like the bottleneck, but I have no first-hand judgment and should be questioned by people who understand robotics
D06.late_modes: Leaderboard-chasing demos of generalized manipulation: without real-robot verification it is a show, and it may fail on a different robot body

D07.one_line: Control has clear test criteria, but the term WAM itself looks like a naming contest, and it is easy to mistake a demo for a paradigm
D07.late_modes: Chasing the name WAM to make demos: a naming and PR contest, and the RoboArena leaderboard-chasing controversy is the signal

D08.one_line: Whether it predicts real outcomes correctly outside the training data is the only criterion that makes sense to me for judging this kind of work
D08.late_modes: Simply chasing more realistic video generation and calling it a world model: generating something that looks right is not the same as predicting correctly
D08.conflict: Meta board member; the V-JEPA series is work from Meta/FAIR

D09.one_line: Computation is cheap and real experiments are expensive and slow; this is the same arbitrage structure I describe for biology experiments

D10.one_line: No judgment: the material contains no judgment of his own on autonomous driving, which is exactly the boundary of his path dependence

D11.one_line: Humans and models still differ by ten-odd to a few dozen points on spatial and visual reasoning, which shows a real unsolved problem and not just a way to publish papers

D12.one_line: Generation aimed at visual realism is the kind that gets commoditized fastest in the sorting machine, and Sora 2 shutting down after six months is a ready-made lesson
D12.late_modes: The race in generation aimed at visual realism: Sora 2 was shut down six months after launch, which shows this route is overtaken quickly

D13.one_line: I trust invariants and hard constraints more than model alignment; this is an engineering habit, not a researched position

D14.one_line: FlashAttention-style academic contributions show that a small team can build infrastructure adopted across the whole industry; this kind of work is underrated
D14.conflict: Stripe acquired OpenRouter, i.e. AI model-routing infrastructure

D15.one_line: The direction he bets on most heavily (Arc): the read-think-write loop has compounding potential, but verification is the real bottleneck; the interest is extremely deep, disclosed only and not adjusted for
D15.conflict: Arc is the institution he co-founded with his wife and has put the most into, a direct bet on AI × biology

D16.one_line: No first-hand material; the cost-effectiveness of trading compute for quality in generative recommendation reminds me of diminishing progress per dollar, but this is only an analogy

lever_reason: Evaluation, meaning who gets to define what good concretely looks like, is my number-one heuristic; next after it are world models, simulation and real data that can be verified in reality; scaling itself is not a lever an individual researcher should bet on

Q2.condition: Narrow-domain model + credible third-party evaluation + a team of 2-4 + months of compute + open weights; missing any one makes it more of an exercise than a real contribution

cruxes.question: Without credible evaluation, can a breakthrough in world models or architectures be recognized and adopted by the outside world?
cruxes.my_position: No; without a measurement anyone can trust, even the best representation is only a claim made in the lab and will not really be adopted downstream
cruxes.would_change_if: A model whose measurement method is widely questioned keeps delivering on its promise in independent real-robot tests or third-party replications

cruxes.question: Can an academic lab with a few dozen GPUs still make a foundation-model contribution that industry will adopt?
cruxes.my_position: Yes, but only in the combination of narrow domain + strong evaluation + open weights; the door to general pre-training has closed
cruxes.would_change_if: Within two years, another case like FlashAttention or DPO appears: something that came from a small team and later became a default industry component

cruxes.question: Is embodied intelligence now stuck on real-robot data and hardware, or on the model algorithms themselves?
cruxes.my_position: I lean toward data and hardware (thin evidence, inferred); this is where my material is thinnest and it should be questioned by people who understand robotics
cruxes.would_change_if: An algorithmic breakthrough that clearly improves cross-embodiment transfer without needing more real-robot data or cheaper hardware

taste_advice: First let your model take one independent test it could lose, and only then talk about how useful it is; do not trust only the ruler you built yourself

pairwise.why: Both are high, but evaluation is the source of verification, and world models too will in the end be tested by it
My material on D06 is too thin; D05 is the direction where my evidence is strongest and I am most confident
D08 at least has concrete work that can be tested (V-JEPA); on D06 I can almost only infer
D08's test criterion (predicting real outcomes) is more fundamental, while D07 easily falls into a naming and demo contest
I can work out the sim-to-real arbitrage structure by analogy with biology; I cannot judge D06 itself
D03's long-horizon credit assignment looks more like a new unsolved bottleneck, while D02 looks more like optimizing a known pipeline
On understanding, the gap between humans and models is still ten-odd to a few dozen points, while generation has already entered sorting-machine-style hyper-competition
The door to pre-training has basically closed to academia, while the door to evaluation is still open
D04's scaffolding is being absorbed by the models themselves, while D03's sample-efficiency problem lasts longer
For D05 I have a more direct framework and evidence; D13 is mostly inference
I am not sure about either, but D10 is locked up more tightly by a few giants and their fleet data, while D06 at least still has open problems
